2. Finance, accounting and economics

Economic profit

Economic profit=Accounting profit−Opportunity costs not recorded\text{Economic profit} = \text{Accounting profit} - \text{Opportunity costs not recorded}Economic profit=Accounting profit−Opportunity costs not recorded
Accounting profit\text{Accounting profit}Accounting profit
Revenue minus expenses as recorded under the accounting rules (net income)$
Opportunity costs not recorded\text{Opportunity costs not recorded}Opportunity costs not recorded
The value of alternatives given up that involve no transaction, such as the owner’s forgone salary and the return her money could earn elsewhere$

Assumes. Both are measured over the same period. The opportunity costs are estimates of what the best alternatives would really have paid.

Operating cash flow (simplified)

Operating cash flow=Accounting profit+Non-cash expenses\text{Operating cash flow} = \text{Accounting profit} + \text{Non-cash expenses}Operating cash flow=Accounting profit+Non-cash expenses
Accounting profit\text{Accounting profit}Accounting profit
Net income for the period$
Non-cash expenses\text{Non-cash expenses}Non-cash expenses
Expenses that used no cash in the period, chiefly depreciation$

Assumes. A simplification: it assumes customers paid in cash, bills were paid as they arose, and stocks of supplies did not change. When they did, timing differences must also be adjusted for.

Assumes. All three are measured at the same moment, in the same currency.

Equity as net assets

Equity=Assets−Liabilities\text{Equity} = \text{Assets} - \text{Liabilities}Equity=Assets−Liabilities

Assumes. Revenue, expenses and dividends are the period’s totals, not yet moved into retained earnings.

Growth rate of average order value

Assumes. Revenue is exactly visits × conversion rate × average order value, which is an identity when the three are calculated from the same visits, orders and revenue.

Step-by-step (sequential) contributions to a change in revenue

ΔV=(V1−V0) c0A0Δc=V1(c1−c0)A0ΔA=V1c1(A1−A0)\Delta_V = (V_1 - V_0)\,c_0 A_0 \qquad \Delta_c = V_1 (c_1 - c_0) A_0 \qquad \Delta_A = V_1 c_1 (A_1 - A_0)ΔV​=(V1​−V0​)c0​A0​Δc​=V1​(c1​−c0​)A0​ΔA​=V1​c1​(A1​−A0​)
V0, V1V_0,\ V_1V0​, V1​
Visits in the earlier and the later periodvisits
c0, c1c_0,\ c_1c0​, c1​
Conversion rate in the earlier and the later period, as a decimal
A0, A1A_0,\ A_1A0​, A1​
Average order value in the earlier and the later period$ per order
ΔV, Δc, ΔA\Delta_V,\ \Delta_c,\ \Delta_AΔV​, Δc​, ΔA​
Change in revenue attributed to visits, conversion and order value, changed in that order$

Assumes. The drivers are changed one at a time in a stated order: visits, then conversion, then order value. Each step keeps the drivers already changed at their new values, which is why the three contributions add up exactly to the change in revenue, V₁c₁A₁ − V₀c₀A₀. Changing each driver alone from the old values gives contributions that do not add up.

M01 Marketing Fundamentals

1. What marketing is

Value created by an exchange, and how the price divides it

V=W−CGain to buyer=W−PGain to seller=P−CV = W - C \qquad \text{Gain to buyer} = W - P \qquad \text{Gain to seller} = P - CV=W−CGain to buyer=W−PGain to seller=P−C
VVV
Value created by the exchange: the total gain to both sides$
WWW
Willingness to pay: the most the buyer would pay for the offer rather than go without it$
PPP
Price paid$
CCC
Seller’s cost of providing this one sale (only the costs the sale causes)$

Assumes. The buyer buys only if P ≤ W and no alternative would leave her more (its own W − P); the seller can keep selling only if P ≥ C. W is the buyer’s own judgement and is rarely known exactly.

2. Customer value, satisfaction and lifetime value

Net value of an offer to a customer (when benefits and costs can be put in money)

Net value=W−(P+N)\text{Net value} = W - (P + N)Net value=W−(P+N)
WWW
Willingness to pay: the most this customer would pay for the offer rather than go without it (the money value of its benefits to her)$
PPP
Price, including any money extras such as delivery$
NNN
Non-money costs put in money: time at the customer’s own value of time, effort, and the expected cost of risk (probability × cost if it goes wrong)$

Assumes. The customer can put a money value on the benefits and on her time and risk. She compares the net value of each alternative, including doing nothing (net value $0), and chooses the highest.

Customer lifetime value (margins at year end; retention constant)

CLV=∑t=1Tm rt−1(1+d)tevery future year: CLV=m1+d−r\text{CLV} = \sum_{t=1}^{T} \frac{m\, r^{t-1}}{(1+d)^{t}} \qquad \text{every future year: } \text{CLV} = \frac{m}{1 + d - r}CLV=t=1∑T​(1+d)tmrt−1​every future year: CLV=1+d−rm​
CLV\text{CLV}CLV
Customer lifetime value: the present value of the margins the customer is expected to bring in$
mmm
Margin per year from the customer: revenue minus the costs that serving them causes (not revenue)$ per year
rrr
Retention rate: the probability that a customer in one year is still a customer the nextdecimal (0.70 = 70%)
ddd
Discount rate per yeardecimal (0.10 = 10%)
ttt
Year of the relationship, 1 for the first yearyears
TTT
Number of years counted (the horizon)years

Assumes. Each year’s margin arrives at the end of the year; the customer is certain to be there for year 1 and stays from one year to the next with the same probability r; m, r and d don’t change; acquisition cost is not included. The short form adds every future year and needs r < 1 + d.

Customer acquisition cost, and the net value of winning a customer

CAC=SnNet value of a new customer=CLV−CAC\text{CAC} = \frac{S}{n} \qquad \text{Net value of a new customer} = \text{CLV} - \text{CAC}CAC=nS​Net value of a new customer=CLV−CAC

nnn
Number of new customers won in the periodcustomers

Assumes. The spending caused the new customers (those who would have come anyway shouldn’t be counted as won by it), and CLV is estimated for the kind of customer the spending wins.
